column2: In that kingdom Bharata consecrated him; the king, having transferred his fortune to his son, entered the forest.
His son too was Tejas, a Prajapati, conqueror of foes; Tejas's learned son is remembered as Indradyumna.
His son was Parameshthin, and at his death his family arose by name, the Pratihara line.
Of that wise one too was born the famed Pratihartri; Pratihartri's Unnetri; his son is remembered as Bhuma.
His son was Udgitha, and his son Prastavi; Prastavi's son Vibhu; his son became Prithu.
Prithu's son was Nakta, Nakta's son Gaya; Gaya's son Nara; Nara's son Virat.
Virat's son was the very mighty Dhiman; Dhiman's son Mahan; Mahan's Bhauvana.
Bhauvana's (son) Tvashtri; his son Viraja; Viraja's son Raja; Raja's Shatajit.
He had a hundred sons, all kings, led by Vishvajyotis, by whom these creatures were increased.
By them this Bharata varsha, with seven continents, is marked here; by those born in their line this Bharati was enjoyed formerly.
Seventy-one yugas named Krita, Treta and the rest have passed; the kings of their lineages passed with those yugas.
Formerly in the Svayambhuva interval, hundreds and thousands. Thus the creation of Svayambhuva, by which this world was filled,
with sages and deities, ancestors, Gandharvas and Rakshasas, Yakshas, beings and Pishachas, humans, deer and birds; their creation is declared, and revolves with the yugas.
From the breadth of Jambudvipa their length is told: two mountains a hundred thousand yojanas long;
Nila and Nishadha; lesser than those are the others: Shveta, Hemakuta, Himavan and Shringavan.
They are extended two thousand ninety... (eighty-two thousand?) yojanas; in their midst are the countries, those seven varshas.
They are surrounded by mountains uneven with precipices, joined by various rivers, mutually inaccessible.
Beings of many kinds live in them everywhere. This Himalayan varsha is famed by the name Bharata.
Beyond this is Hemakuta, remembered by the name Kimpurusha; beyond Hemakuta is Naishadha, called Harivarsha.
Beyond Harivarsha, in Meru's... is Ilavrita; beyond Ilavrita, the Nila, famed by the name Ramyaka.
Beyond Ramyaka is the white, famed as Hiranmaya; beyond Hiranmaya, Shringavat, Kuru is remembered.
The two varshas, south and north, should be known as bow-shaped; four long ones are there, and the middle is Ilavrita.
This side of Nishadha is remembered the southern half-altar; beyond Nilavat is the northern half-altar.
In the southern half-altar three varshas, and in the north three; between them is Meru, the middle, Ilavrita.
South of Nila and north of Nishadha extends a great mountain named Malyavan.
A thousand yojanas, extending to Nila and Nishadha; its length is declared thirty-four thousand.
West of it is to be known the mountain Gandhamadana; by length and breadth it is famed as like Malyavan.
In the middle of two circles stands Meru, the golden mountain, four-coloured, golden, square and lofty.
Sumeru shines white, attended as by kings, with the colour of the young sun, like a smokeless fire.
It is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, plunged sixteen below and spread sixteen.
Because it is shaped like a bowl, it spreads thirty-two at the top; its circumference all round is three times its breadth.
By circular measure the measure is desired in triangular form: forty thousand yojanas all round
increased by eight; the triangular measure is declared. By square measure the circumference all round
is ordained as sixty-four thousand yojanas. That mountain, very divine, is joined with divine herbs,
wholly covered with auspicious dwellings made of gold. There all hosts of gods, Gandharvas, serpents and Rakshasas
and auspicious troops of Apsarases are seen on the king of mountains. That Meru is surrounded by worlds that nurture beings.
Four countries are established on its four sides: Bhadrashva, Bharatashva, Ketumala in the west,
the northern Kurus, refuge of those who have done merit; and on the side of Gandhamadana is the western hillside,
lovely in all seasons, always delighted, auspicious, thirty-two thousand yojanas from east to west,
in length thirty-four thousand by measure. There the Ketumalas of auspicious deeds are established.
There all the men are black, greatly sattvic, very mighty, and the women are like lotus petals, all of pleasing appearance.
There is a great divine tree, a jackfruit, the support of six flavours, the lord, Brahma's son, going at will, swift as mind.
Drinking the juice of its fruit, they live for a great span. By the side of Malyavan, in the east, is the unprecedented hillside;
by length and breadth like the western hillside. The Bhadrashvas there are to be known as always glad in mind.
There is the forest Bhadrashala, and the Kalamra, a great tree. There those men are white, greatly energetic, endowed with strength;
the women are lily-coloured, beautiful, pleasant to see, with moon-like radiance and colour, faces like the full moon,
with limbs cool as the moon, those women smelling of lotuses. Their lifespan, free of disease, is ten thousand years.
Drinking the juice of the Kalamra, all have stable youth. South of Shveta and north of Nila
is the varsha called Ramanaka; humans are born there, devoted to love, spotless, free of old age and foul smell,
endowed with white pedigree, all pleasant to see. There too is a very great tree, a great red banyan;
drinking the juice of its fruit they sustain themselves, ten thousand and fifteen hundred years.
They live, those fortunate ones, always seen, best of men. South of Shringavat and north of Shveta
is the varsha named Hairanvata, where the river Hairanvati flows. Mighty, very radiant humans are born there,
Yakshas, heroes, of great being, wealthy, pleasant to see; those greatly vigorous ones live eleven thousand years,
a lifespan of one thousand and fifteen hundred; in which varsha is a great tree, the lakucha, support of six flavours.
Drinking the juice of its fruit they live without disease. Shringavat has three great high peaks:
one of jewels, one of gold, and one of all jewels, adorned with mansions.
North of Shringavat and south of the ocean are the Kurus; that varsha is holy, frequented by Siddhas.
There the trees have honey fruits, with constant flowers and fruit; clothes and ornaments are produced in their fruits.
Some charming trees there grant all desires; they drip the best honey with perfume, colour and flavour.
Others there are charming trees called Kshirins, which constantly drip milk of six flavours like nectar.
The whole ground is jewelled, with fine golden sand, endowed with happiness in all seasons, free of mud, free of dust, auspicious.
Fallen from the world of gods, auspicious humans are born there, endowed with white pedigree, all with stable youth.
Pairs are born, women equal to Apsarases; they drink the milk of those milk-trees, like nectar.
A pair is born at once and grows up equally; conduct, form and affection are equal.
Devoted to one another, with the nature of chakravakas, free of disease and grief, they always enjoy happiness.
They live thirteen thousand and fifteen hundred years, very mighty, and do not resort to other women.
Tungaprastha, Krishnagiri, Godhana, Pushpagiri, Ujjayanta, and Mount Raivataka,
Shriparvata, Chitrakuta, Kutashaila and Giri; others, unknown to them, are small and live scantily.
Mixed with them are countries, Aryas and Mlecchas in portions. By them are drunk these rivers: Ganga, Sindhu, Sarasvati,
Shatadru, Chandrabhaga, Yamuna, Sarayu, Airavati, Vitasta, Vipasha, Devika, Kuhu,
Gomati, Dhutapapa, Budbuda, Drishadvati, Kaushiki, Tridiva, Nishthivi, Gedaki,
Chakshu and Lohita: these issue from the foot of the Himalaya. Vedasmriti, Vedavati, Vritraghni, Sindhu,
Varnasha, Nandana, Sadanira the great river, Pasha, Charmanvati, Anupa, Vidisha, Vetravati,
Kshipra and Avanti: these are remembered as resting on Pariyatra. Shona the great river, Narmada, Surasa, Kriya,
Mandakini, Dasharna, Chitrakuta likewise, Tamasa, Pippala, Shyena, Karamoda, Pishachika,
Chitropala, Vishala, Banjula, Vastuvahini, Sanerujā, Shuktimati, Mankuti, Tridiva, Kratu:
these rivers born of Riksha have jewelled waters, auspicious. Tapi, Payoshni, Nirvindhya, Srpa and the river Nishadha,
Veni, Vaitarani, Kshipra, Vala, Kumudvati, Toya, Mahagauri, Durga and Annashila:
these rivers born of the foot of Vindhya have holy waters, auspicious. Godavari, Bhimarathi, Krishnaveni and Banjula,
Tungabhadra, Suprayoga, Bahya and Kaveri: rivers flowing south issued from the foot of Sahya.
Kritamala, Tamraparni, Pushpajati, Utpalavati: rivers born of Malaya, all cool-watered and auspicious.
Trisama, Rishikulya, Banjula, Tridiva, Abala, Langulini, Vamshadhara are remembered as daughters of Mahendra.
Rishikulya, Kumari, Mandaga, Mandagamini, Kripa and Palashini are remembered as born of Shuktimat.
Those rivers are all Sarasvatis, all Gangas going to the sea, mothers of the universe, remembered as removers of the world's sin.
They have other tributaries by hundreds and thousands. On them live these: Kurus, Panchalas, Shalvas, Madreyas, Jangalas,
Shurasenas, Bhadrakaras, Bodhas, Patacharas, Matsyas, Kushalyas, Saushalyas, Kuntalas, Kashis, Koshalas,
Godhas, Bhadras, Karingas, Magadhas with Utkalas: these Middle-country peoples are mostly proclaimed here.
At the northern edge of Sahya, where the Godavari flows, that region is delightful in all the earth.
There is the city called Govardhana, built by Rama; trees dear to Rama, heavenly, and divine herbs
were planted for his pleasure by the sage Bharadvaja; hence that region of the earlier city became delightful.
Bahlikas, Vatadhanas, Abhiras, Kalatoyakas, Aparantas, Muhmas, Panchalas, Charmamandalas,
Gandharas, Yavanas, Sindhu-Sauvira districts, Chinas, Tusharas, Pallavas, mountain-cave dwellers,
Shakas, Bhadras, Kulindas, Paradas, Vindhyachulikas, Abhishahas, Ulutas, Kekayas, Dashamalikas,
Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra families, Kambojas, Daradas, Barbaras, Angalauhikas,
Atris, with Bharadvajas, Prasthalas, Dasherakas, Lamakas, Talashalas, Bhushikas with Ijikas:
these are the northern countries; learn the eastern ones: Angas, Vangas, Cholabhadras and the tribes of Kiratas, Tomaras, Hamsabhangas, Kashmiras, Tanganas,
Jhillikas, Ahukas, Hunas and Darvas,
Andhravakas, Mudgarakas, Antargiris and Bahirgiris; then the Plavangavas are known, Maladas, Malavartikas,
Samantaras, Pravrisheyas, Bhargavas, Gopa kings, Pragjyotishas, Pundras, Videhas, Tamraliptakas,
Mallas, Magadhas, Gonardas: the eastern countries are remembered. Now the other countries, dwellers of the southern path:
Pandyas, Keralas, Cholas, Kulyas, Setukas, Mushikas, Kshapanas, Vanavasikas,
Maharashtras, Mahishikas, and Kalingas everywhere, Abhiras with Aishikas, Atavyas, Saravas,
Pulindas, Vindhyamauliyas, Vaidarbhas with Dandakas, Paurikas, Maulikas, Ashmakas, Bhogavardhinas,
Konkanas, Kuntalas, Andhras, Kulindas, Angaras, Marishas: the southern countries; learn the western ones:
Suryarakas, Kalivanas, Durgalas, Kuntaras, Pauleyas, Kiratas, Rupakas with Tapakas,
Karitis and all the Karandharas, Nasikas and others, and the Antaranarmadas,
Sahakachchhas, Samaheyas with the Sarasvatas, Kachchhipas, Surashtras, Anartas with Arbudas:
these are the Aparantas; hear the Vindhya dwellers: Maladas, Karuthas, Mekalas with Utkalas,
the Dasharnas of the best, Bhojas with Kishkindhakas, Toshalas, Koshalas, Traipuras, Vaidishas,
Tuhundas, Barbaras, Shatpuras with Naishadhas, Anupas, Tundikeras, Vitihotras, Avantis:
all these countries dwell on the back of Vindhya. Now I shall tell the countries dependent on mountains:
Nihiras, Hamsamargas, Kupathas, Tanganas, Shakas, Apaprāvaranas, Urnas, Darvas with Suhuhukas,
Trigartas, Mandalas, Kiratas with Tamaras. Four yugas in the Bharata varsha, the sages said:
Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Tishya; I shall tell their creation fully later.
South is Nila and north Nishadha; between them the great Meru is established by its own measure.
As it plunges into all the mountains, so its breadth is that measure; its length is remembered as a niyuta.
From the circular form of the sea, from the nature of the earth's disc, the lengths are diminished; they are remembered as equal to the square.
Splitting the four-cornered Ilavrita through the middle, the river Jambu-rasavati flows, like split collyrium.
On the south side of Meru and north of Nishadha, the great eternal jambu tree called Sudarshana stands,
ever with flowers and fruits, frequented by Siddhas and Charanas. Jambudvipa is famed by the name of that tree.
The height of that king of trees is a thousand and a hundred yojanas, touching heaven on all sides.
The measure of its fruit has been counted by the truth-seeing sages as eight hundred sixty-one aratnis.
Falling on the earth, they make a vast sound. The juice of the fruit of that jambu spreads, becoming a river,
circumambulates Meru and enters beneath the jambu root. In Ilavrita it is always drunk, the jambu juice, by those always seen.
When the jambu-fruit juice has been drunk, old age does not trouble them, nor hunger, fatigue, death or sloth.
There the gold called Jambunada, ornament of the gods, arises, shining like cochineal insects.
The auspicious juice of all varsha trees is praised; it falls and becomes that white gold, ornament of the gods.
Their urine and faeces in all directions everywhere, by Ishvara's grace the earth swallows, and the dead too.
Rakshasas, Pishachas and Yakshas are all remembered as Himalayan; on Hemakuta are the Gandharvas with hosts of Apsarases to be known.
On Nishadha are all the Nagas, Shesha, Vasuki and Takshaka; on the great Meru thirty-three gods worthy of sacrifice sport.
On Nila, made of lapis lazuli, are Siddhas and pure Brahmin sages; the white mountain is called that of Daityas and Danavas.
Shringavat, best of mountains, is the resort of ancestors. In the nine white varshas, standing each in its portion,
beings are settled, moving and fixed. Their increase is seen in many ways, divine and human; counting cannot be counted nor believed by those who wish to be.
Its breadth is twice the breadth of Krauncha-dvipa; it stands surrounding the ocean of curd-whey.
There the countries are holy and people die only after a long time; how then famine, and where fear of old age and disease?
There too are seven white mountains adorned with jewels, mines of gems, and rivers; hear their names from me.
The first is called Meru, joined with divine sages and Gandharvas; extending east, golden, the mountain named Udaya.
Clouds there come and go for rain. West of it is the great mountain Jaladhara,
from which Vasava always takes the supreme water; from that rain arises in the rainy season among creatures here.
North of it is Raivataka, where always established is the star Revati in heaven, an ordinance made by the Grandfather.
West of it is the great mountain called Shyama, from which formerly these creatures became dark.
West of it is the great Ajata-Astagiri, remembered; west of that Ambikeya, Durgashaila, the great mountain;
beyond Ambikeya the lovely, with all herbs, Kesari with filaments, from which the wind, the Prajapati, (arises).
From Udaya the first varsha is remembered as the great Jalada; the second of Jaladhara as Sukumara.
Of Raivata, Kaumara; of Shyama, Manivaka; of Asta too, the auspicious varsha is to be known as Kusumottara.
Of Ambikeya, Modaka; of Kesara, Mahadruma; the measure of the continent is small and long.
It is famed as the Krauncha-dvipa; its banner is the great tree called Shaka, of great height, whose great followers are worshipped.
There the holy countries are joined with the four varnas, and the very holy rivers, the Ganga, are sevenfold:
Sukumari, Kumari, Nalini, Venuka, Ikshu, Venuka and Gabhasti the seventh.
